cl_gen_gateway.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether using cannabis makes people more likely to go on to other illegal drugs (the 'gateway' idea), or whether the usual order of first use, and the link between the two, come from a shared liability to use drugs and from which drugs people are offered first. In several observational samples, cannabis use usually came before other illegal drugs and was associated with more use of them. The order differed across countries, including some with moderate cannabis use; these patterns alone do not identify a cause. In New York State public high schools in 1971–1973 (5,468 students linked over 5 to 6 months, 66% of the students surveyed in the fall; students who could not be linked had used more drugs), 26% of the 558 students whose drug use had reached cannabis went on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, mostly pills (12 percentage points) or psychedelics (9), with heroin about 2, against 4% of 2,911 students who had used only legal drugs and 1% of 482 who had used none; 56% stayed at cannabis and 19% used only legal drugs in the interval. These percentages were weighted for the survey design and response, not adjusted for other characteristics. The paper calls cannabis a crucial step in both the abstract and the body, but also says a drug does not invariably lead to the next and that the stages are probably culturally determined (Kandel, 1975). In four US household surveys (1991–1994; 44,624 people aged 12 to 25; ages recalled in whole years; people compared within neighbourhood and survey year, with sex, race or ethnicity and age group adjusted for, plus age at first cannabis use in the cocaine models, but without individual-liability covariates in the described analysis), people who had used cannabis were more likely to have had a first chance to try cocaine (relative risk 4.6, 95% CI 3.8 to 5.6, without alcohol or tobacco use; 7.6, 6.9 to 8.4, with it; against people who had used none of the three) and, once offered, about 15 times as likely to start as people who had not used cannabis, regardless of alcohol or tobacco history (11.3 to 19.8), also when the 73% who reported starting at the same age as their first offer were left out (20.4, 10.2 to 40.7); this exclusion also removed people who accepted an unbidden offer at once, so it did not isolate active drug-seeking; about half of the people who had used cannabis started cocaine within 2 years of a first offer, against under 10% of the others many years later (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). In Australian twins born 1964–1971 (311 same-sex pairs in which one twin, but not the other, recalled first using cannabis before 17; interviewed at about 30), the twin who started early more often reported later use of other drugs (for example cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% against 26.4%, conditional odds ratio 4.19, 95% CI 2.60 to 6.75; hallucinogens 5.15; sedatives 2.83; opioids 2.57); the odds ratios stayed between 2.3 and 5.2 after adjustment for measured differences between the twins, and between 2.3 and 3.9 (unadjusted) in the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis. The within-pair comparison accounts for shared rearing, but identical and fraternal pairs were pooled, so genetic confounding is controlled only partly. Separate identical-pair estimates were not printed; peer affiliation and temperament were not described as measured covariates in this paper, without establishing what the broader register measured; the authors call the results consistent with a causal role, perhaps through the social setting of cannabis use and access to other drugs, and say that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from them alone (Lynskey et al., 2003). A simulation of US young people, calibrated to household surveys of 1982–1994, in which one shared liability brings forward both the chances to use and the use of all drugs and cannabis has no effect by design, reported a strong relative risk of using heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens (157 in the model, against 24 in the surveys). The survey ratio compares use of those drugs by 21 between people who had and had not used cannabis by 21, without requiring cannabis first; the model’s description also uses prior-initiation wording, so the two ratios may not measure exactly the same quantity. The model also produced an order in which those drugs rarely come first (11 per 1,000, against 16 in the surveys) and a rise with cannabis frequency, and adjusting for an imperfect measure of that liability left large associations; it shows that these patterns cannot by themselves identify a cause, but it was not compared with a model that includes one, and its authors think something like a gateway effect probably exists through contact with illegal markets (Morral et al., 2002). In the 17-country WHO programme (2001–2005; ages recalled at one interview), the order varied across countries alongside how common each drug was. Among people who had used other illegal drugs by 29, cannabis had not already been used at their first other-drug use in 11.4% in the USA and 12.7% in New Zealand, against 83.2% in Japan and 77.8% in Nigeria, where cannabis was rare; these definitions include people who never used cannabis. The Japan and Nigeria estimates rested on just 16 and 8 people using other drugs, with 13 and 7 in the not-already-cannabis groups (unweighted counts alongside weighted percentages). The corresponding proportion was also high in South Africa (59.2%), where the authors call cannabis use moderate, and Mexico (48.4%). The observed correspondence does not show that prevalence caused the order. In pooled interaction models, the link of cannabis with later other drug use was weaker where cannabis was more common, while that of alcohol or tobacco with later other drug use was stronger where those were more common; the Netherlands–USA country contrast alone does not demonstrate that prevalence relationship; and starting in an unusual order was largely unrelated to later dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). A narrative review by proponents of a shared liability argues that the order need not reflect causal steps and calls that liability empirically proven. It also argues that the cannabis-to-other-drug association itself is negligible after accounting for cannabis prevalence, citing a book rather than presenting new data for that assertion. It cites classical twin studies but does not discuss discordant co-twin-control evidence (Vanyukov et al., 2012). No study read separated a causal effect, a shared liability and access to drugs in one design, and all their data were collected between 1971 and 2005. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
cl_gen_gateway.plain: Does using cannabis lead to other drugs? This is not known. In many places studied, most people who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis first. This was not the order for everyone. Cannabis use was also linked to more use of other drugs: in New York schools in the early 1970s, about 1 in 4 students who had used cannabis tried another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, against 4 in 100 of those who had used only alcohol or tobacco. In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often used other drugs later than the other twin, The comparison accounts for growing up in the same home, but not all genetic or other differences between twins. A computer model showed that the same pattern appears if some people are simply more likely to use any drug and are offered cannabis first, with no effect of cannabis at all. Across surveys in 17 countries, the order varied. Some people had not used cannabis when they first used another illegal drug, including some who never used cannabis. This was common in some places with rare or moderate cannabis use; the estimates for Japan and Nigeria came from very few people. No study separated cause, shared risk and access to drugs. See the contested question.
cl_gen_gateway.magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Kandel (1975), 5–6 months, unadjusted: moved beyond cannabis 26% of 558 students at the cannabis step (pills 12, psychedelics 9, cocaine 2, heroin 2 percentage points) vs 4% of 2,911 who had used only legal drugs and 1% of 482 who had used none; started cannabis 27% (N≥342) after beer or wine, cigarettes and hard liquor vs 2% (N≥467) after no drug. Wagner & Anthony (2002), relative risks (95% CI): first chance to try cocaine, against people who had used none of alcohol, tobacco or cannabis, 1.9 (1.7–2.1) after alcohol or tobacco only, 4.6 (3.8–5.6) after cannabis only, 7.6 (6.9–8.4) after both; starting cocaine once offered, cannabis vs no cannabis, 15 (11.3–19.8), and 20.4 (10.2–40.7) without people who started in the same year as the offer (73% of people who used cocaine); about 50% of people who had used cannabis started within 2 years of a first offer vs under 10% of others many years later. Lynskey et al. (2003), 311 discordant pairs, twin who started cannabis before 17 vs co-twin, lifetime prevalence and conditional odds ratio, unadjusted (adjusted): sedatives 19.0% vs 8.4%, 2.83 (2.28); hallucinogens 35.4% vs 18.0%, 5.15 (5.15); cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% vs 26.4%, 4.19 (4.06); opioids 13.5% vs 6.4%, 2.57 (2.34); in 234 pairs in which both used cannabis, unadjusted 3.00, 3.92, 3.00 and 2.33. Morral et al. (2002), simulation with no gateway effect vs US surveys: reported relative risks157 vs24; the survey uses cannabis and other-drug use by21 without requiring an order, while the model also uses prior-initiation wording, so exact comparability is uncertain; one of those drugs at least a year before cannabis, 11 vs 16 per 1,000; odds ratio 297 with no adjustment, 82 after adjustment for a liability indicator correlated0.8 with the liability (64% variance in a simple linear reading; editors’0.8² calculation, not80%); no uncertainty intervals. Degenhardt, Dierker, et al. (2010): people who had not already used cannabis when starting other illegal drugs by29 (including never-cannabis use), USA 11.4%, New Zealand 12.7%, Japan 83.2% (13 of 16 people), Nigeria 77.8% (7 of 8); cannabis and later other illegal drugs at 18–29, odds ratio 7.4 (1.8–30.4) in the Netherlands vs 107.1 (57.9–198.1) in the USA; pooled interaction of cannabis use with cannabis prevalence 0.3 (0.2–0.6), of alcohol or tobacco use with their prevalence 32.7 (8.3–129.0), scale not stated.

cl_gen_polydrug.statement: As summarized in two narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand and come from studies the reviews did not appraise, using more than one drug is common among people who use illegal drugs, how common depends on who was asked and how use was defined, and it makes the long-term effects of any one drug hard to study in people. Studies define it as using several drugs over a period (lifetime, or the past 1 to 12 months) or on the same occasion, the second being hard to capture in surveys and mostly studied in smaller high-risk samples, although the review also describes national survey work that measured same-occasion use; the historical DSM diagnosis of polysubstance dependence was dropped from DSM-5, and most population research records only how often each drug is used. Studies that group people by the drugs they use typically find a limited range (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis), a moderate range (adding amphetamine-type drugs) and an extended range (adding prescription drugs used non-medically and other illegal drugs). Limited-range use was reported by 18% of 12- to 17-year-olds (ever) and by 34% of teenagers before 16, in two samples; extended-range use by 2% of 12- to 17-year-olds and 13.5% of 18- to 29-year-olds in Australian national samples, two different age groups that the review calls panel designs; and up to 75% of people at underground raves used several drugs, on average five at the last rave. Classes with a wide range of use reported more psychological distress, anxiety and depression in cross-sectional studies; several imaging studies and studies of inhibitory control and decision-making found no difference in performance from comparison groups, while another study reported large differences on standard tests outside the scanner and a metabolite study linked brain measures with memory performance. The findings were mixed, although the review’s conclusion states cognitive deficits as clear; and the authors judged research on preventing and treating the use of several drugs underdeveloped (Connor et al., 2014). In the ecstasy research reviewed in 2006, the great majority of people who used it also used other drugs, most often alcohol, cannabis and stimulants: earlier studies found cannabis use in 90% to 100% of people who used ecstasy, and in one survey everyone new to ecstasy (1 to 9 pills in all) had smoked cannabis in the previous month, 32% on five or more occasions. Studies that compared people who use ecstasy with people who use no drugs therefore make it difficult to separate ecstasy from other drug effects; in studies with comparison groups who used other drugs but not ecstasy (samples described as up to234, without resolving whether this counts only people using ecstasy or all comparison groups), raised psychological problems went with drug use in general rather than with ecstasy, though those comparison groups mostly used drugs more moderately; some earlier studies did not record other drugs; and findings on whether cannabis explains, adds to or offsets problems seen in people who use ecstasy pointed in different directions. The reviewers propose following young people at risk from before they start using drugs, for years, with drug histories recorded and psychological and cognitive tests repeated (Gouzoulis-Mayfrank & Daumann, 2006). How often people who use cocaine also drink or use cannabis, and what that means for cocaine research, is in the answer on cocaine with alcohol and cannabis. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
cl_gen_polydrug.plain: How common is using several drugs, and why does it matter? It is common among people who use illegal drugs, according to two reviews whose figures are second-hand. In Australian surveys, 2 in 100 teenagers and about 13 in 100 young adults used a wide range of drugs; at underground raves, up to 75 in 100 people used several drugs, five on average at the last rave. In ecstasy studies, 90 to 100 in 100 people also used cannabis, and many also drank alcohol or used stimulants. This makes it hard to know what one drug does over time: studies of people who use ecstasy may be measuring several drugs at once, and some older studies did not record the other drugs. The cocaine page has the figures for cocaine with alcohol and cannabis.
cl_gen_polydrug.magnitude: As described, not pooled, no intervals. Connor et al. (2014): limited-range use 18% of 12–17-year-olds (lifetime) and 34% of teenagers before 16; extended-range use 2% at 12–17 and 13.5% at 18–29 (Australian national samples of different age groups; 13.2% in the review's annotation of one source); up to 75% of people at underground raves using several drugs, on average five at the last rave; a sedative-and-alcohol class with last-year prevalence 1.3% among young Australian adults. Gouzoulis-Mayfrank & Daumann (2006): cannabis use in 90–100% of people who used ecstasy in earlier studies; in one survey all people new to ecstasy (1–9 pills) had smoked cannabis in the previous month, 32% on five or more occasions; comparison studies with up to 234 people who used ecstasy.
